synopsis: ACAS X is the successor to TCAS and an aviation advisory function with the pilot remaining in the loop, so it is a precedent for collision-warning logic rather than automatic braking [f1428, f1435, f15748]. Validation focused on threat-resolution logic, using simulation as primary evidence: millions of simulated encounters represented billions of flight hours, while pilot assessment and flight evaluation remained part of validation [f1907, f1432, f1571, f1911]. This capability took years to build from real radar data; the European CREME encounter model drew on twelve million flights, and a MIT Lincoln Laboratory model used nine months of radar data [f1909, f1430, f1433]. RTCA, EUROCAE and aviation authorities accepted ACAS X evidence, and its DO-385 and ED-256 minimum operational performance standards were published in October 2018 [f1912, f1429]. The booklet treats this as evidence that statistical simulation can be accepted for a safety-critical collision function, but emphasizes the prerequisite investment in encounter models and unresolved sensor-noise disagreements; the validation duration after capability became available was not found [f15756, f1257, f1910].
